newsitem.title: CANADA: CWB says watching costs to US PNW and Gulf ports.
newsitem.headline: CWB says watching costs to US PNW and Gulf ports.

text.p: The Canadian Wheat Board is monitoring the cost of shipping Canadian grain to U.S. ports in the Pacific Northwest and Gulf of Mexico from the Prairies, a CWB spokesman said.

"We're monitoring the cost through these different (U.S.) port areas and generally they're not favourable from a cost point of view but we'll be looking at them a little closer over the next month because of the transportation problems we're having," CWB spokesman Norm Cobb told Reuters.
Thirty-eight ocean vessels waited to load grains at Canada's Pacific ports on Wednesday. One ship waited 41 days.
"If the cost is within a few dollars or some range, we might decide to ship through those ports," Cobb said.
The state grain exporter said it faces C$15 million in demurrage fines because of the delays since early January and passed on new sales for February and March shipment.
Canadian National Railway and CP Rail System will add more locomotives to move the more than 28,300 hopper cars in their combined fleets, Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale told Reuters.
Pacific terminal elevators will operate seven days a week begining March 1, Goodale said.
The CWB shipped one train load of grain through the U.S. to Portland, Ore., during the March 1995 port strike in Vancouver, Cobb said.
The agency also shipped grain to Latin America last summer through U.S. Gulf ports, a CWB statement has said.

"We haven't made any moves yet but we may be considering that if the situation doesn't alleviate somewhat. Generally, it would be a more expensive solution than shipping through the Canadian system," Cobb said.
Rail costs through the U.S. range between C$7 to C$30 a tonne more, he added.
Asked whether U.S. rail costs closer to the low end of that range could entice Canadian grain movement to American ports, Cobb said: "Yes."
